w:r.w:t: Visitor Portal → APIs → Database → Host → Approval → Reception → Face → Gate → Exit → Reporting

Purpose: one practical document showing exactly how the VMS should be developed module-by-module, how portals connect to APIs, how APIs connect to services/database/devices, and how the complete visitor lifecycle is assembled.

Source basis: the supplied VMS SDD defines the 15-module architecture, dependency order, end-to-end lifecycle, API baseline, database domains, security rules and 18-week implementation plan. Exact physical ERD keys/cardinality and final payload schemas remain detailed-design items in the source.

VMS is one application platform with multiple user interfaces. Visitor Portal, Host Portal, Reception Console, Gate Console, Security Console and Admin/Reporting screens must not become separate business systems. They all call the same VMS backend.
Backend = authentication, authorization, business rules, workflow and access decision.
Device adapters = gate, camera, printer and other hardware/API boundaries.
Audit = traceability of important business/security actions.
This is the main flow the development team should keep visible throughout the project:
Backend validates site, access zone, schedule and permissions.
Visitor receives invitation and completes required registration/consent/documents.
Reception or gate looks up the visit.
Identity/QR and face verification are performed where configured.
Backend evaluates policy, time window, watchlist, zone and document requirements.
Only ALLOW can activate physical access.
Entry transaction is stored; occupancy and host notification are updated.
Visitor exits; access is disabled; visit closes.
Audit and reports expose the complete lifecycle.

Do not develop the modules randomly. The supplied SDD's dependency model starts with authentication/RBAC, then core visitor/visit data, host/visitor portals, workflow, notifications/badge, reception/face, security/access, and finally reporting/integration.

face, access-controller, notification, SSO, camera, printer
auth, visitor, host, reception, gate, security, admin, reports
Create core identity, organization, visitor, visit, approval and configuration domains.
Add foreign-key integrity for core relationships.
Index visitor identity/contact, visit date/status, active visits, gate transactions and audit timestamp/type.
Keep sensitive biometric references logically separated where practical.
Server-side authorization on every protected endpoint.
External integration calls go through adapters.
Build this before the other portals because every portal needs identity and permissions.
Add administrator MFA/stronger authentication where configured.
Tests: authentication success/failure, expired session, disabled user, insufficient permission, SSO failure and RBAC negative tests.
Before creating a real visit, the system needs the master data against which that visit will be validated.
This is the transaction core. Keep Visitor and Visit separate.
Links visitor + host + site + schedule + purpose + access requirements.
Used by approval, reception and gate validation.

State model should be finalized during detailed design; the implementation baseline uses the flow DRAFT → PENDING_APPROVAL → APPROVED/REJECTED → EXPECTED → CHECKED_IN/INSIDE → CHECKED_OUT/CLOSED, with expiry/exception handling.
The host portal is the main pre-arrival business interface.
Search existing visitor or create visitor.
Enter visit purpose, date/time, site and access zone.
Backend validates permissions and business rules.
Backend creates approval task when required.
Host monitors pending/approved/rejected/expired status and history.
The visitor portal should collect information and complete the authorized invitation flow. It should not decide whether a physical gate opens.
Backend validates visit state and authorization.
Show QR/pass only after the backend confirms the visit is authorized.
Typical APIs: /visitors, /visits, consent/document operations, invitation/pass operations.
Approval is a backend state machine, not a frontend-only status.
Backend validates that the transition is legal.
Persist actor, time, decision and remarks.
This is where approval matrix, time-window rules and escalation belong.
Notifications are downstream effects of business events.
Notification failure must not silently change the visit authorization. Keep provider-specific SMTP/SMS logic behind a notification adapter.
Build digital/printed pass generation and badge validity.
The QR/pass represents an authorized visit; it is not by itself the final physical access decision.
If not found and walk-ins are allowed, create a walk-in.
Contact host/approver if confirmation is required.
Check in only after successful validation.
Use controlled manual/degraded mode when camera/network/device/face service fails.
Important: existing-visit and walk-in flows must converge before final CHECK-IN so walk-ins cannot bypass security rules.
Face recognition is a separate service boundary.
Generate/store protected biometric reference according to the approved design.
Send result to the VMS access decision engine.
Mismatch/liveness failure → retry or controlled alternate verification.
The face service must not directly open a gate. It is an input to the VMS business decision.
Security administrators manage restricted visitor rules. Gate validation checks applicable restrictions before ALLOW.
This is the most security-sensitive flow.
Check access zone and document/policy conditions.
Return ALLOW / DENY / HOLD with reason code and correlation ID.
Only ALLOW may invoke the physical controller. DENY/HOLD must not open the gate.
Audit is cross-cutting. The responsible backend service should generate the event.
Build reporting after the operational transaction model is working.
Keep external systems behind adapters so the VMS business logic does not depend on one vendor's SDK.
The supplied architecture explicitly separates integration concerns from the core application.
Every portal follows the same pattern:
UI → API /api/v1 → Auth/RBAC/Validation → Controller → Domain Service → Repository → MySQL/Object Storage → External Adapter when required → Audit → Response.
Visitor UI must not call Host UI directly.
Gate UI must not connect directly to MySQL.
React must not directly operate the access controller.
Normal application APIs must not return raw biometric templates.
Notification provider failure must not change authorization.
Use this template for every backlog item:
Define the UI screen and fields.
Define DB tables, keys, indexes and migration.

Example: Host creates visit → Create Visit screen → POST /visits → Visit Controller → Visit Service → validate visitor/site/zone/time → DB → Approval Service → Notification → Audit → Host status screen.
Real device/API integration tested before pilot.
Architecture, security zones, integration boundaries, environments, API standards
ERD, API contracts, RBAC, state machine, audit, face contract, UI/UX
Repo, CI/CD, DEV/QA, auth, RBAC, master data
Freeze SDD/API/ERD/RBAC/state model before full implementation.
Complete visitor + visit + host + visitor portal flow.
Complete face service and integrate it with visit validation.
Run SIT → UAT → NFR → Pilot → Production.
Keep every feature traceable: Requirement → UI → API → Service → DB → Integration → Audit → Test.

All portals are different user interfaces, but there is one VMS backend that owns authentication, business rules, workflow, database transactions, access decisions and audit; specialized face/device/external services connect through controlled APIs and adapters.
